The expression in the lesson is character-for-character the one in the source.

git show stage-1:DonHang.Api/Dtos.cs lines 1-13 match the lesson's block exactly, including both comment lines: `public sealed record ProductDto(int Id, string Name, int PriceVnd);`, `OrderItemDto(int ProductId, int Quantity, int UnitPriceVnd)`, `OrderDto(int Id, int CustomerId, string Status, DateTimeOffset PlacedAt, List<OrderItemDto> Items)`, `CreateOrderItemRequest(...)`, `CreateOrderRequest(List<CreateOrderItemRequest> Items)`. The file continues past line 13 with `LoginRequest`/`LoginResponse` (see issue on section 5).

git show stage-1:DonHang.Domain/Entities.cs — `public sealed class Product { public int Id { get; set; } public required string Name { get; set; } public int PriceVnd { get; set; } }`. Exactly three properties, no others.

Entities.cs: `public sealed class OrderItem { public int OrderId; public int ProductId; public int Quantity; public int UnitPriceVnd }` (all `{ get; set; }`). Dtos.cs: `OrderItemDto(int ProductId, int Quantity, int UnitPriceVnd)` — OrderId is the only dropped field. OrdersController.ToDto maps `i => new OrderItemDto(i.ProductId, i.Quantity, i.UnitPriceVnd)`, and OrderItemDto appears only nested in OrderDto.

Entities.cs: `public sealed class Customer { public int Id; public required string FullName; public required string Email; public required string City; public string? PasswordHash }`. PasswordHash exists and is nullable (comment: "Null until the customer sets a password"); the lesson's section 6 wording ("alongside a customer's name and email") is accurate, City also present.

ASP.NET Core docs, Format response data (moniker >= aspnetcore-7.0, so it governs 10.0): "configures PascalCase formatting instead of the default camelCase formatting". .NET docs, Configure options: "Web defaults for JsonSerializerOptions ... PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase". The CamelCase policy is "First word starts with a lower case character. Successive words start with an uppercase character" (TempCelsius -> tempCelsius) - not "lowercase the first letter"; and it is ASP.NET Core's web defaults, not System.Text.Json's own default, that turn it on.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: ASP.NET Core's default JSON options for Web API controllers set a camelCase naming policy, so a C# property name is written camelCase in JSON: the first word starts lowercase and later words keep their capital (`PriceVnd` → `priceVnd`). System.Text.Json used on its own, outside these web defaults, leaves the C# name as written.

issues.quote: one JSON field filling one property, the exact reverse of serialization
issues.text: Unlisted claim: deserialization is called "the exact reverse of serialization", which no claim in the ledger covers and which the pinned behaviour contradicts. ASP.NET Core's web defaults set PropertyNameCaseInsensitive = true, so a body with `PriceVnd`, `pricevnd` or `priceVnd` all bind to the same property — reading is not the mirror image of writing, which applies one fixed camelCase policy. Docs: "Web defaults for JsonSerializerOptions … PropertyNameCaseInsensitive = true".
issues.fix: Replace with: "one JSON field filling one property — the same field-by-field mapping, run the other way." Drop "exact reverse", and add a claim to .meta.json for the deserialization direction (version_key aspnetcore) citing the web-defaults list.

issues.quote: `DonHang.Api/Dtos.cs` holds every shape an endpoint answers in or reads from
issues.text: Unlisted claim, and false for stage-1 as written. Error bodies are a shape endpoints answer in and are not in Dtos.cs: Program.cs calls `builder.Services.AddProblemDetails()` and ExceptionHandlingMiddleware writes `new ProblemDetails { Status, Title, Detail }` with content type application/problem+json; `NotFound()` in ProductsController/OrdersController answers with no DTO at all.
issues.fix: Narrow the sentence to what is true, e.g.: "`DonHang.Api/Dtos.cs` holds the shapes these endpoints answer in and read from, kept in one file separate from `DonHang.Domain`'s entities". Then add it to .meta.json as a fact claim pointing at DonHang.Api/Dtos.cs @ stage-1.

issues.text: The block is verbatim for lines 1-13, but Dtos.cs at stage-1 is 17 lines: it also declares `public sealed record LoginRequest(string Email, string Password);` and `public sealed record LoginResponse(string Token);`. Combined with the prose "holds every shape", a reader who opens the file finds two records the lesson presented as absent.
issues.fix: Keep lines=1-13, but say the excerpt is partial — e.g. "the first records in the file" — or note that the same file also holds the sign-in shapes used later. Do not extend the block: LoginRequest/LoginResponse belong to the auth-basics module.

issues.quote: ASP.NET Core's default serializer lowercases the first letter of each property name for JSON
issues.text: Two imprecisions repeated in sections 3, 4, 6, the five-line summary and quiz q3's explanation. (1) The rule is a camelCase naming policy — "First word starts with a lower case character. Successive words start with an uppercase character" — not a first-letter rule; a name whose first word is an acronym does not behave as stated. (2) It is ASP.NET Core's web defaults (PropertyNamingPolicy = CamelCase) that enable it; System.Text.Json on its own keeps the C# name unchanged.
issues.fix: Say "ASP.NET Core's default JSON options write each property name in camelCase — the first word lowercase, later words keeping their capital: `PriceVnd` becomes `priceVnd`", and mirror that wording in sections 3, 6, summary line 4 and quiz q3's explanation.

issues.quote: returning the entity directly serializes it too, unless it happens to be null for every customer tested
issues.text: Key `a` is still the only defensible answer, but its condition and the scenario context are wrong for the pinned defaults. ASP.NET Core does not set DefaultIgnoreCondition, and System.Text.Json writes null properties unless WhenWritingNull is opted into, so `return Ok(customer)` emits `"passwordHash":null` even for a customer with no password. The context's "a JSON object with `id`, `fullName`, `email`, and `city`" therefore cannot happen, and the explanation's "manual testing … would miss it entirely" is backwards.
issues.fix: In the context, list the observed fields as `id`, `fullName`, `email`, `city` and `passwordHash: null`, or say the tested customers have no password set yet and the field shows as null. Change option a to "…serializes it too — it appears as `passwordHash` in every response, null or not" and fix the explanation to match.

issues.quote: A DTO is not the entity; something in the endpoint's own code has to build one from the other, field by field.
issues.text: "entity" is never defined. Core concepts says a DTO is kept separate from "whatever internal type the server uses", then section 4 switches to "the entity" and section 5 to "DonHang.Domain's entities" without saying the two words mean the same thing. I can guess it, but the lesson's whole point is DTO-versus-entity, so I am guessing at the main idea.
issues.fix: In the Core concepts DTO bullet, name it once: "...kept separate from the internal type (the entity) the server uses for the same thing."

issues.quote: **DTO** (data transfer object) — a plain type shaped for the wire, holding only the fields a client needs
issues.text: "shaped for the wire" / "on the wire" is jargon I have not met. It carries the definition of the one term this lesson teaches, and it is also in the title and in summary line 1, so I cannot skip it. The rest of the bullet ("only the fields a client needs") is what actually told me something.
issues.fix: In the DTO bullet, gloss it in place: "shaped for the wire — for the JSON that travels in a request or a response —".

issues.quote: Each `record` here is a type whose only job is to hold these named values — a shape, not behavior.
issues.text: The block declares `public sealed record ProductDto(int Id, string Name, int PriceVnd);` and the prose calls it "named values", but nothing says the names inside the parentheses ARE the type's properties. Everything after this depends on that: "one JSON field per property", "three fields, matching ProductDto's three properties", and quiz q3/q4. I had to assume it.
issues.fix: After "a shape, not behavior", add one sentence: "Each name in the parentheses is one property of that type — that is the list serialization walks."

issues.quote: it is what the serializer does to every property, every time, unless told otherwise.
issues.text: "unless told otherwise" opens a door and shuts it. I do not know whether telling it otherwise is something I will have to do, or how, and I spent time wondering whether I had missed it earlier in the lesson.
issues.fix: Replace "unless told otherwise" with "and nothing in this lesson changes it", so I know there is nothing missing.

issues.quote: Property names do not survive that trip unchanged going out.
issues.text: The camelCase rule is carefully limited to "going out", and the paragraph before it says a request body's JSON fills a `CreateOrderRequest`. So if I send a body myself, do I write `items` or `Items`? The text raises the question by saying "going out" and never answers it, and Try it only exercises a response.
issues.fix: Add one clause after "going out": say whether the same camelCase names are what an incoming body is expected to use, or say that incoming names are not covered here.

issues.quote: `ProductsController.List()`, from the last lesson, does exactly this: `new ProductDto(p.Id, p.Name, p.PriceVnd)`
issues.text: `ProductsController.List()` and the fragment `new ProductDto(p.Id, p.Name, p.PriceVnd)` are not in this lesson's code block, and `p` is never named. The following clause ("read off a `Product` row") lets me work out that `p` is the row, but only after a second read.
